data.title: PM Modi to launch development projects worth ₹34,470 cr in Bihar's Vaishali
data.description:
Prime Minister Narendra Modi will visit Bihar's Vaishali district on Saturday to launch projects worth nearly 34,470 crore, including a six-lane bridge over the Ganga river, and address a public meeting, officials said.

This would be the Prime Minister's first visit to the eastern state since May, when he had attended a function marking the expansion of the cabinet headed by Chief Minister Samrat Choudhary, the first BJP leader to lead a government in Bihar.

Elaborate security arrangements, including the suspension of vehicular movement on the national and state highways concerned for a stipulated period, have been made in Vaishali and Patna for the PM's visit, they said.

 

The 9.76-km-long six-lane bridge, which connects Bidupur block in Vaishali to Kachchi Dargah on the outskirts of Patna, has been named 'Nitish Setu', in deference to the former Bihar chief minister, on whose watch the project was conceived and came close to completion.

"The PM will visit 'Nitish Setu' in Vaishali. Thereafter, at around 2 pm, he will inaugurate and dedicate to the nation various development projects and lay the foundation stone of several projects, worth around Rs 34,470 crore altogether," an official said.

However, the naming of the bridge has triggered a war of words between the ruling NDA and the main opposition party RJD, which has shared power with Nitish Kumar, albeit briefly, and seeks to claim its own share of credit.

The projects span road connectivity, energy, urban infrastructure, water resources, education, healthcare, transport and other important sectors, and are aimed at strengthening infrastructure and improving public services across the state.

The PM will flag off 100 PM-eBuses, giving a further boost to cleaner public transport in the state.

Griha Pravesh ceremonies for over 26,900 beneficiaries under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (Urban) will also be held, marking an important milestone in providing housing to urban families, another official said.

data.title: CERT-In flags unauthorised payment transactions, warns of AI cyberattacks
data.description:
India's cyber agency said on Friday it had reported unauthorised transactions at service providers ​for banking and financial services entities, ​and also at technology service providers supporting government-linked payments.

Payment fraud incidents extended beyond the financial sector to vendors and partner payout platforms, cyber agency CERT-In said in an advisory on Friday.

Attackers altered business records or approval relationships and then used legitimate payment processes, it said. It did not say how much money had been improperly paid out, or by whom.

The agency ‌also said that it identified the use of AI-driven frameworks in cyberattacks across different sectors, and issued several recommendations for government organisations, non-financial payout platforms and technology service providers.

 

India has seen a spate of cyberattacks on banks and non-bank lenders ​in recent weeks, even as authorities issued warnings and the Reserve Bank of ‌India tightened cybersecurity checks.

Earlier this month, CERT-In named the hacking group behind a ​wave ‌of AI-driven attacks on financial firms and identified its tools, ‌at least two of them linked to China.

Late last month, India's central bank warned banks ‌of ​rising cyberattacks on ​financial infrastructure, seeking proof of compliance with existing rules and details of their preparedness for ‌AI-related risks.

data.title: Nvidia employees accused Huang of abusive conduct in 2007 lawsuit
data.description:
By Brian Baxter (BLAW), Maggie Eastland and Ian King
 
About two decades ago, two Nvidia Corp. employees complained about how then-Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang treated his staff, including allegations that he threatened them and made sexually explicit remarks, according to allegations contained in a California lawsuit filed in 2007. 
Stephen Pettigrew, the first in-house lawyer hired by Nvidia, said he observed Huang regularly verbally abusing and intimidating employees, according to court documents filed in the Superior Court of California. Pettigrew alleged he was fired for raising concerns about the conduct of Nvidia executives, while the company cited performance issues for his termination, according to court documents.
 
 
“He would scream at them, threaten them with extreme bodily harm and make sexually oriented comments while thrusting his hips in a demonstration of the sex act,” according to a brief filed by Pettigrew’s attorneys in a lawsuit alleging age discrimination and wrongful termination. The dispute, in which Nvidia brought counterclaims against Pettigrew seeking the return of corporate documents, was resolved through a confidential settlement in December 2009.
 
Another employee, Michael Winston, the senior vice president for human resources, filed a discrimination complaint in 2005 alleging he was fired after objecting to “Huang’s abusive treatment of employees, including conduct he believed constituted sexual harassment,” according to court documents from Pettigrew’s lawsuit, which contain some details from Winston’s complaint.
 
The behavior of Nvidia’s founder toward his employees, even decades ago, is front of mind for many as he appeals to the board to let him return to the position he occupied for more than three decades. He resigned earlier this month following disclosures of multiple affairs including with a direct report and a suspected Chinese spy whose relationship with Huang is being investigated by the US Justice Department. Huang himself has admitted to “torturing” those who work closely with him to make sure they deliver their best work, and news stories have surfaced about him allegedly demeaning subordinates during his extended tenure running the company.
 
He has never fought characterisations of being harsh and has, at times, publicly shown that side of his personality. 
 
A representative for Huang said, “These false allegations are from over 20 years ago and were made by two fired employees. The thousands of employees who have shown support for Jensen over the last week show they are false.”
 
Nvidia representatives didn’t respond to requests for comment. Details of the complaints were previously reported by the New York Times.
 
Huang, 63, has explained his approach as being motivated by a sense of crisis and needing to move forward quickly in a rapidly changing technology industry. He has often expressed his pride in not laying off staff and regretted the one time he did so. 
Some of his Silicon Valley allies are supporting the effort to reinstate Huang, and so are some Nvidia employees, according to an anonymous poll that says it reflects their responses. So far, the board and senior management have publicly rejected the prospect Huang coming back.
 
In the vast majority of his appearances outside of Nvidia or at events open to the public, he behaves in a congenial, often lighthearted and joking way and makes time for people. While he was at Nvidia, those who reported to him maintained a reverential demeanor when discussing him, even while admitting that he could be fearsome.
 
Both Pettigrew and Winston are deceased, and several attorneys representing them and family members couldn’t be reached for comment.
 
A former electrical design engineer who previously worked at three large law firms, Pettigrew joined Nvidia in September 1999 after the company went public earlier that year. He was fired in June 2006.
 
In his lawsuit, Pettigrew sought more than $2.6 million in damages from Nvidia, and the company at one point tried to settle the case for $175,000, according to court records. In the court filings, Pettigrew described wrongdoing by an unnamed “senior executive at Nvidia” who allegedly made sexual remarks and threatened to rip off an employee’s arm off and beat them with it. The executive also allegedly said, “If that’s your business plan, then bend over and drop your pants.”
 
A trial brief in Pettigrew’s case cited the discrimination complaint filed by Winston, which Pettigrew received from California’s Department of Fair Employment and Housing while working for Nvidia in 2005, according to court records. Depositions in Pettigrew’s case stated that Winston, who was hired by Nvidia in September 2004, spent only four weeks at the company. 
 
Nvidia reached a confidential settlement agreement with Winston for more than $1 million, according to the New York Times.
 
Winston would subsequently make a name for himself as a would-be corporate whistleblower, with a jury awarding him $3.8 million in damages from Countrywide Financial Corp. after he claimed the company fired him for raising concerns about its lending practices. A federal appeals court overturned that award.

data.title: Over 27 weddings, 12K guests: Traffic curbs likely on roads in South Delhi
data.description:
Traffic congestion is expected on several roads in South Delhi on Saturday, with more than 27 marriage functions scheduled across the area, drawing over 12,000 guests and an estimated 5,000 additional vehicles, police said.

The functions are scheduled on SSN Marg (Bhati Mines Road), Bandh Road, Mandi Road and MG Road.

The affected stretches include SSN Marg, 100 Foota Road, Anuvrat Marg, Aurobindo Marg, Mandi Road, Jonapur Road, Mehrauli-Gurugram Road and Mehrauli-Mahipalpur Road, the Delhi Traffic Police said in an advisory.

Adequate traffic personnel have been deployed to regulate vehicular movement in the area, it said.

Commuters have been advised to avoid these roads, wherever possible, and use the Delhi Metro to save time and fuel.

 

They have also been asked to plan their journeys in advance and check the traffic police's social media handles for live updates and diversions.

Wedding guests have been requested to park their vehicles only in designated parking areas and avoid roadside parking.

The traffic police helpline number is 1095, while emergency assistance can be sought by dialling 112.

data.title: Dutch court bars Chinese SUV in Europe over resemblance to JLR Defender
data.description:
A Dutch district court in The Hague on Friday issued an injunction barring European Union sales of a large SUV made by China's BYD , saying it infringes on ​the design of Jaguar Land Rover's popular Defender model.

JLR, a unit of India's ​Tata Motors, launched the case earlier this year after BYD announced on its UK website that the seven-seater ‌Ti7 SUV was available for orders with deliveries to customers starting in January 2027.

BYD launched the Fangchengbao Ti7 in China last year.

The Defender is JLR's most popular model, with global sales of over 100,000 units in 2025.

"In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover," the court ruling said. "The characteristic and distinctive elements of the design are reflected in the BYD Ti7."

 

According to automotive media, among the visual similarities between the two vehicles are a boxy, flat-roof silhouette, upright proportions, tailgate styling, squared-off wheel arches and a solid body-colored panel behind the rear passenger door.

The injunction will take effect a week after the ruling because BYD "currently has no concrete plans to place the ‌Ti7 on the market in the EU."

Until the intellectual property case is resolved, the court also banned BYD from producing the vehicle at its new factory in Hungary, which is due to start mass-producing cars early next year.

The judge ruled, however, that the court had no jurisdiction over BYD's affiliate in the United Kingdom.

It is rare in Europe for major automakers to go to court over design rights infringement. It is also uncommon for such a ruling to come so early in proceedings of a case that is ongoing and likely to last for ​some time.

"We protect our intellectual property and take legal action when necessary," JLR said in a statement. "Legal proceedings are ongoing, ‌and we won't be commenting further at this time."

Legacy automakers have often complained that Chinese automakers have copied designs, though little has been proven in court. In 2005, for instance, General Motors and Chinese ​rival Chery settled ‌a case over the Chery QQ that the No. 1 US automaker said was a copy of its Chevrolet Spark.

In ‌a statement, BYD said it "strongly disagrees" with the ruling and will appeal it.

"The BYD Ti 7 is the result of BYD's own independent design work and infringes none of JLR's rights," BYD said. "We will pursue every ‌legal ​avenue to demonstrate ​that this decision is incorrect."

BYD has grown rapidly in Europe since launching sales on the continent in late 2022. According to ACEA data, the Chinese automaker's sales more than doubled to over 280,000 ‌vehicles in Europe this ​year through September over the same period last year, outselling Ford, Tesla and Nissan.

data.title: Russian missiles, drones land in Poland, Nato calls it a 'violation'
data.description:
Two Russian missiles and a suspected drone came down in Poland on Friday in what its prime minister said was likely a provocation timed to coincide with European military exercises in his country for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine.

The incidents occurred while Russia carried out a major nighttime bombardment of neighbouring Ukraine. The development stoked tensions between Europe and Moscow just as the US tries to add momentum to talks it is mediating on ending the war that began with Russia's all-out invasion of Ukraine nearly five years ago.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared that "we are dealing with an intentional provocation" by Russia.

 

There was no immediate comment from Moscow on the missiles and suspected drone, or on Friday's drills.

One Russian missile is believed to have crashed around 35 kilometres (22 miles) from where the military exercises were taking place, officials said. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down roughly 50 kilometres (30 miles) from the Ukraine border, and what officials believe was likely a jet-powered drone hit about 30 kilometres (20 miles) from the border with Ukraine.

There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage.

European troops were taking part Friday in an unprecedented two-week military exercise that began Nov. 9 in southeastern Poland. Forces are preparing for a possible postwar mission in Ukraine aimed at helping to stabilize the country and rebuild its military.

European countries previously have expressed alarm at what they deem to be Russia's attempts to destabilize the continent.

US President Donald Trump discussed the war at a summit in China on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, according to his envoy Steve Witkoff. Another envoy, Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, told European leaders that the United States believes Russia is "comfortable" with Nato-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, in what could be a step toward compromise.

Russia's nighttime attack on Ukraine came hours after Putin vowed to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes this week on a bridge linking occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. The bridge is vital to Moscow's war effort.

Nato chief addresses a grave violation' by Russia Images from closed-circuit cameras and a mobile phone in the region collected by Poland's PAP news agency showed a large, loud explosion and a bright flash, apparently in a wooded area, in one of the crashes.

Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the development in Poland a "grave violation" of that country's airspace. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," Rutte wrote on X.

Rutte is expected to go to Poland this weekend in response.

Under Nato's collective security guarantee Article 5 of its founding treaty an attack on any ally should be considered an attack on all 32 members. It obliges members to provide support to that ally, most likely military backup, but does not limit them to that alone.

Article 5 is not triggered automatically. Ultimately, it is a political decision that all members must agree to. Poland also has the option to enact Article 4, which it did last year. This provides for emergency consultations only.

The development brought a chorus of European condemnation.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham described it as "utterly unacceptable." European Council President Antonio Costa said that Russia "continues to spread (its) threats." Germany's Foreign Ministry called it "yet another example of Russia's ongoing provocations." Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the incident in Poland "demonstrates the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the trans-Atlantic community." Putin has said that Russia will not accept any European troops deployed to Ukraine after a prospective peace deal and will view them as legitimate targets.

Russian attacks batter Ukraine, killing at least 8 Overnight strikes killed at least eight Ukrainian civilians and wounded more than two dozen, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Russia fired more than 400 drones and over 110 missiles, 27 of them ballistic and some carrying cluster warheads that scatter dozens of smaller bomblets across a wide area, he said.

The attack fit the pattern of Moscow's heavy responses to eye-catching Ukrainian attacks, such as the ones this week on the Kerch Bridge, and added to uncertainty about the prospects for ongoing talks brokered by Washington.

Russia and Ukraine are still far apart on the possible terms for a peace deal.

Russia takes aim at Ukraine's missile and drone plants Russia's Defence Ministry said the sites it hit Friday were linked to the Ukrainian military. It said it hit a facility where missiles are assembled, a plant making components for rocket fuel, and a facility where drones are assembled.

Ukraine said the deadly attacks also wounded more than a dozen people as apartment blocks, medical facilities, warehouses and three bridges took hits.

Russia's nighttime barrage also extended its campaign to knock out Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter. Strikes on power plants, substations and transmission lines forced Ukraine's three operational nuclear power plants to reduce generation, bringing emergency outages in 11 regions, said Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov.

data.title: Virginia's first measles-related fatality in 2026 takes US death toll to 12
data.description:
Virginia has reported its first measles-associated child death of 2026 after a young child who tested positive for the highly contagious disease died, taking the nationwide death toll from measles to 12 this year.

The Virginia Department of Health announced the death on Friday, stating that the child was between the ages of zero and four. However, officials did not disclose the child's exact age or provide further details, citing the need to protect the family's privacy, ABC News reported.

"There has been a recent increase in measles activity in some areas of Virginia," the department said in a news release on Friday.

 

The department urged residents to take preventive measures to protect themselves and their communities from the disease and avoid further fatalities.

The latest death comes amid a rise in measles infections across the United States. According to ABC News, other measles-associated fatalities this year have been reported in New York, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.

The development also comes days after the Pan American Health Organisation announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status after maintaining it for more than 25 years.

The country first declared measles elimination in 2000, indicating that the virus was no longer spreading continuously within its borders. However, the status is lost when the same strain of the virus circulates continuously for 12 months or longer.

According to the latest data from the US Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the country has recorded 5,838 confirmed measles infections this year, with cases reported in nearly every state.

Children and teenagers aged 19 and below account for the majority of infections, while approximately one in six children under the age of five who contract measles require hospitalisation.

CDC data further shows that around 96 per cent of reported cases involved individuals who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown.

The CDC recommends two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine, with the first administered between 12 and 15 months of age and the second between four and six years. One dose provides 93 per cent protection against measles, while two doses offer 97 per cent protection.

data.title: Saudi-led coalition strikes Houthi targets as rebels attack Saudi Arabia
data.description:
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen said Friday that its forces struck targets used by the rebels to smuggle and transport weapons, while the rebels attacked neighboring Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

The exchanges came days after the Saudi-led coalition launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen.

In Gaza, Israeli strikes killed six people, health officials said. Israel's military said it attacked militants.

In Iraq, army troops and police who protect the country's energy industry deployed to a city south of the capital after the government apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia that it had accused of smuggling oil there.

 

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.

Israeli strikes in Gaza kill 6, local health officials say Israeli strikes killed six people in central Gaza on Friday, according to health officials at Gaza's Awda hospital and Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital, where the casualties were taken.

An overnight strike killed one person in the Nuseirat Refugee camp, while a second strike killed another person in the city of Deir Al-Balah Friday afternoon. A third strike killed four people in the Bureij Refugee camp on Friday evening.

Israel's military confirmed attacking "militants" in a few strikes in central Gaza, without elaborating.

Saudi Arabia says it targeted Houthi smuggling operations The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said Friday it targeted the rebels' operations to smuggle and transport weapons and ballistic missiles in Yemen's main Red Sea port of Hodeidah.

It added that it had carried out a military operation in Yemen's rebel-held capital of Sanaa early Friday, targeting the Houthis' military capabilities to prevent attacks on civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi-led coalition also said the kingdom intercepted five drones and one ballistic missile fired by the rebels Friday morning. Riyadh, the kingdom's capital and largest city, was among the targets.

A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, claimed in a statement that the rebels attacked Jazan's port in Saudi Arabia and a power station in the Al-Shuqaiq area in Jazan. The Saudi-led coalition had earlier acknowledged that debris from intercepted missiles fell in the Al-Shuqaiq area, but did not immediately report any damage.

The interceptions came a day after the Iran-backed rebels said they had targeted Saudi airports, air bases and Riyadh's financial center.

Iraqi forces deploy to area known as Iran-backed militia stronghold Iraqi security forces set up a command headquarters Friday on the outskirts of the Jurf al-Sakhar area south of Baghdad, as they aim to assert control over a longtime stronghold of an Iran-backed militia, Kataib Hezbollah.

Tensions had flared after the government called for the militia to withdraw amid allegations that it was using the area for oil smuggling. Kataib Hezbollah had threatened to fight security forces if they attempted any incursion.

Two Iraqi officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly, said the government and Kataib Hezbollah had reached an agreement under which security forces could enter but the militia would not immediately withdraw.

The deal followed negotiations facilitated by Esmail Qaani, commander of Iran's Quds Force, a branch of the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard that's responsible for operations outside Iran and is key to Iran's influence and ties to allies across the Middle East.

Under the agreement, the Iraqi army, federal police and energy sector police are deploying to the area. In a compromise, the deployment also includes fighters from the Popular Mobilization Forces, a collection of mostly Shiite armed groups close to Iran that are officially part of Iraq's security forces. Kataib Hezbollah would withdraw its fighters within a month.

Oil flowing nearly to pre-war levels, despite increase in attacks, analysts say Substantial amounts of oil continue to flow to the global economy from Mideast producers despite a recent increase in Iranian attacks on shipping, energy analysts say.

Around 80 per cent of the prewar amount of oil is being exported, most of it through the Strait of Hormuz under the protection of US forces. Oil also is transported through pipelines leading to ports on the Red Sea and the Gulf of Oman that tankers can reach without making the dangerous run through the strait.

Oil flows in the first two weeks of November fell by around 20 per cent to around 13 million barrels per day compared to October, when exports roughly equalled the prewar amounts of 15-16 million barrels per day, according to Rystad Energy.

Reasons for the November decline include Iranian attacks that discourage tankers from attempting the strait crossing, and reduced flows through a key Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu that has been attacked several times.

Somalis protest 'Emirati aggression' in Mogadishu Hundreds of demonstrators in Somalia's capital accused the United Arab Emirates of sowing division in the coastal East African nation by supporting breakaway regions and armed groups opposed to the government.

The protest late Thursday evening in Mogadishu came after Somali officials announced they were expelling the UAE's ambassador, accusing the country of violating Somalia's sovereignty.

The UAE has faced accusations of interference in several African countries, including Sudan. Somalia is a strategic priority for outside powers, in part due to its location across the Gulf of Aden from Yemen, putting it along critical shipping routes connecting Gulf Arab states to global markets.

data.title: Anthropic researcher claims AI helped solve 150-year-old Riemann hypothesis
data.description:
By Elena Eisenstadt and Rachel Metz
 
On the heels of Anthropic PBC’s record-breaking initial public offering, a researcher at the company said he believes he used its artificial intelligence software to solve a famous number theory problem that has plagued mathematicians for more than 150 years. 
Mathematician Levent Alpöge published a note on his personal website on Friday, claiming to have come up with a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. He shared a link to code written in the programming language Lean that he said showed evidence of his success. 
 
According to his note, Alpöge messaged Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei on Sunday night to ask about announcing his findings to the public. Alpöge called the timing of his announcement “horrible,” but said, “I just could not live if I waited even longer.” Anthropic declined to comment, and Alpöge did not respond to a request to comment.
 
 
The Riemann hypothesis relates to the distribution of prime numbers and has long been considered one of the most difficult math problems in the field.
 
OpenAI and Anthropic have been working for years to demonstrate the advanced capabilities of their most cutting-edge models by solving challenging math and life sciences problems. 
 
If confirmed, Alpöge’s work would mark the second Millennium Prize Problem that may have been solved by AI; OpenAI said its models had generated a solution to the 90-year-old Navier-Stokes problem in September. 
 
Andrew Sutherland, a senior research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said he verified Alpöge’s work about the Riemann hypothesis on his computer and has seen at least three other verifications on multiple systems from other professional mathematicians.
 
Alpöge’s efforts with Claude build on the work of many mathematicians who have studied the Riemann hypothesis, as well as the field of mathematic formalization, according to Sutherland.
 
“I am both very nervous and very excited” for the future, Sutherland said, explaining that mathematicians have years ahead to dig into this proof to understand how it can be applied. “This is a day for celebration,” Sutherland said, even as he acknowledged the concerns in his field about AI’s potential impacts the math profession and other jobs.
 
Noah Giansiracusa, an associate professor of math at Bentley University and faculty associate at Harvard University, added that, if the solution works, it’s a big deal for AI.
 
“It sounds like there’s a pretty good chance this is airtight and valid,” Giansiracusa said.
 
Alpöge described the experience of attempting to prove the problem as a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt.” 
 
“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote.

data.title: US court sentences Nikhil Gupta to 235 months jail in Pannun murder plot
data.description:
Indian national Nikhil Gupta was sentenced to 235 months in jail by a US federal judge on Friday for his involvement in a murder-for-hire plot against a Sikh extremist on American soil.

US District Judge Victor Marrero in the Southern District of New York announced the verdict.

Gupta, 55, had pleaded guilty earlier this year to charges of murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering, in connection with his efforts to murder Khalistani separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.

Pannun, who holds dual American and Canadian citizenship, was present in the court when the verdict was announced.
